title: Tech stock sell-off sparks fears the AI trade is on its last legs
excerpt: A jarring sell-off across tech is rewiring the thinking on where the AI trade goes from here, as uncertainty builds heading into 2027.
content_html:
Wall Street forecasters are starting to worry that the AI trade is on its last legs

By Jennifer Sor

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-20T21:02:06.238Z

Wall Street is staring at a sea of red in tech and AI names since the market climbed to all-time highs barely a month ago.

A bruising weekslong sell-off in tech stocks sent the Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the year on Friday, while dragging the S&P 500 and the Dow into a correction.

Now, more Wall Street forecasters are posing a tough question for investors: is the AI trade over?

Concerns about the end of the artificial intelligence-fueled bull market have picked up amid the bloodbath in the tech sector. Selling has been driven by panic about slowing AI capex, the "blunami" midterms and the impact on data centers, and the Nvidia crisis that's now taken the stock down by 47% since early October.

Most recently, Anthropic's IPO came and went without making a positive impact on the broader market. The record public offering was expected to give the AI sector a much-needed boost, and the market's mixed reaction is the latest evidence that the AI trade is struggling.

The Nasdaq 100 is inching closer to an official bear market. The tech-heavy index is down 17% from its all-time high earlier this year, but many corners of the tech sector are already in bear territory.

More painful losses are being felt in the chips, memory, data center, and neocloud sectors.

InvestmentPeak-to-trough losses
(as of November 20)
Global X Data Center & Digital Infrastructure ETF-30%
iShares Semiconductor ETF-37%
Roundhill Memory ETF-58%
Roundhill Neocloud ETF-63%

Wells Fargo is flagging the risk of a broader valuations reset in the AI space, the bank wrote this week, triggered by factors like higher rates, elevated oil prices, signs of economic weakness, and tighter regulation of AI, Sameer Samana, the head of global equities and real assets at the bank, told Business Insider.

Samana said the market's reaction to this week's mega-IPO from Anthropic supported the bank's view that the AI sector could be in the midst of a reset. He declined to give an estimate of how much stock prices could fall, but laid out one hypothetical where earnings growth cratered by 33%, leading valuations to fall in suit.

"The IPO is sucking a lot of liquidity from other parts of the market," he said, adding that the bank favored large-cap communication services, industrials, and materials stocks to avoid becoming "overly reliant on the AI story."

"We expect volatility to remain elevated as markets reassess AI spending, regulation, industry leadership, and the conversion of investment into free cash flow," the note added.

With Anthropic's IPO in the rearview, investors are turning their attention back toward AI capex, with many wondering if spending will continue to hold up and justify mega valuations in the tech space.

A major fear brewing is that data center spending will slow in the next year as lawmakers crack down on new construction, capping growth in the sector.

Investment research firm TS Lombard said it changed its stance on global equities to "underweight," trimming areas exposed to AI in the US and Taiwan. The firm added that it is "sceptical" of the idea that the market can avoid an AI crash altogether, and in a separate note, it laid out a scenario where the market sees a "definite vibe shift" by the end of 2027, resulting in a 40% crash in AI-linked stocks by early 2028 as tech firms slash capex guidance.

"The question was whether AI could generate the massive, unprecedented revenues that could justify those multi-trillion-dollar investments, particularly when the underlying tech was now freely available and most regular people just weren't that fussed. By early 2028, the answer to that question was a resounding 'no,'" strategists wrote of their hypothetical scenario.

Capital Economics, a research firm that has long warned of an AI bubble, pointing to the risks around AI revenue and investment. The firm predicted the S&P 500 dropping 9% through the end of next year in a note following Anthropic's IPO, though the index could post even steeper losses in the interim.

"The revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding. And a combination of the other risks, even in minor form, looks plausible: for example, somewhat stricter regulation of the buildout and application of AI, plus a tightening of AI-related financing," researchers wrote.

"A stock market AI bust in 2027 has long been our central forecast and appears to be a growing concern for investors," the firm added.

Citi said it cut its risk exposure to US equities last month and, in a note this week, advised investors to remain on guard. The bank highlighted spillover risks related to Nvidia, given that the chip giant backstops a wide range of data center projects, neocloud providers, and AI firms.

Jensen Huang's departure is also being viewed by some investors as a nearly existential risk, given that Huang served as the unofficial poster child of the AI trade.

"AI risks have been rising," analysts wrote, adding that the rotation in stocks recently resembled the "extreme" moves leading up to the burst of the dot-com bubble.

Others are taking issue with the sheer magnitude of tech's decline from record highs.

The prominent AI researcher Gary Marcus pointed to losses all over the tech sector in his newsletter, Marcus on AI, on Friday. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF, for instance, is down 24% from its summertime peak.

"In the coming months (if not days) Nvidia and the Neoclouds will get hit hard," Marcus wrote in a note on Substack. "It is very much looking like the death spiral that this newsletter has long warned about has begun."

With Anthropic's IPO in the rearview, investors are turning their attention back toward AI capex, with many wondering if spending will continue to hold up and justify mega valuations in the tech space.

A major fear brewing is that data center spending will slow in the next year as lawmakers crack down on new construction, capping growth in the sector.

Investment research firm TS Lombard said it changed its stance on global equities to "underweight," trimming areas exposed to AI in the US and Taiwan. The firm added that it is "sceptical" of the idea that the market can avoid an AI crash altogether, and in a separate note, it laid out a scenario where the market sees a "definite vibe shift" by the end of 2027, resulting in a 40% crash in AI-linked stocks by early 2028 as tech firms slash capex guidance.

"The question was whether AI could generate the massive, unprecedented revenues that could justify those multi-trillion-dollar investments, particularly when the underlying tech was now freely available and most regular people just weren't that fussed. By early 2028, the answer to that question was a resounding 'no,'" strategists wrote of their hypothetical scenario.

Capital Economics, a research firm that has long warned of an AI bubble, pointing to the risks around AI revenue and investment. The firm predicted the S&P 500 dropping 9% through the end of next year in a note following Anthropic's IPO, though the index could post even steeper losses in the interim.

"The revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding. And a combination of the other risks, even in minor form, looks plausible: for example, somewhat stricter regulation of the buildout and application of AI, plus a tightening of AI-related financing," researchers wrote.

"A stock market AI bust in 2027 has long been our central forecast and appears to be a growing concern for investors," the firm added.

Citi said it cut its risk exposure to US equities last month and, in a note this week, advised investors to remain on guard. The bank highlighted spillover risks related to Nvidia, given that the chip giant backstops a wide range of data center projects, neocloud providers, and AI firms.

Jensen Huang's departure is also being viewed by some investors as a nearly existential risk, given that Huang served as the unofficial poster child of the AI trade.

"AI risks have been rising," analysts wrote, adding that the rotation in stocks recently resembled the "extreme" moves leading up to the burst of the dot-com bubble.

Others are taking issue with the sheer magnitude of tech's decline from record highs.

The prominent AI researcher Gary Marcus pointed to losses all over the tech sector in his newsletter, Marcus on AI, on Friday. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF, for instance, is down 24% from its summertime peak.

"In the coming months (if not days) Nvidia and the Neoclouds will get hit hard," Marcus wrote in a note on Substack. "It is very much looking like the death spiral that this newsletter has long warned about has begun."
